newsitem.title: JAPAN: Norilsk move casts doubt on Russian PGMs for Japan.
newsitem.headline: Norilsk move casts doubt on Russian PGMs for Japan.

text.p: Russian platinum group metal (PGM) shipments to Japan, already delayed by several months, have been thrown further into doubt by news that Russia"s Norilsk wants to sell its output directly, traders said on Tuesday.

A Norilsk spokesman said on Monday that the financially troubled group wants to sell its platinum, palladium and related metals directly to end users, rather than selling to the state PGM export agency at a discount to world prices.
"We see from the news that a turf war is breaking out in Russia regarding jurisdiction over PGM sales," said Naoya Suga of Ishifuku Metal Industry Co Ltd, a major Japanese bullion house.
"If so, shipments of platinum group metals are likely to be postponed further," he said.

Russia"s platinum group export agency Almazjuvelirexport (Almaz) told Reuters and several Japanese trade houses last week that, following the February 12 approval of the Russian budget by the upper house of parliament, Japan-Russia talks on PGM shipments for 1997 would probably be held in March.
As a result, traders in Tokyo concluded that shipments from Russia could resume in April or May.
But Japanese traders said there had been no word from Almaz so far this week on a schedule for talks in Japan. Almaz currently controls all Russian PGM exports.
"We thought the Russian mission would arrive in Japan by the end of March. But the situation may have changed from last week," said a source at a major Japanese trading house.
Japan and Russia, respectively the leading consumer and leading producer of the PGM palladium, usually hammer out one-year PGM contracts in mid-December for shipments beginning the following January.

The talks for 1997 shipments were delayed by uncertainty over the Russian budget, forcing Japanese traders to buy palladium in the spot market and fuelling a speculative rally that last week took prices to 10-month highs above $140 an ounce.
Prices eased after the Russian budget was passed, and at 0500 GMT on Tuesday spot palladium was quoted at $134/$135.
Uncertainties about the Russian export agency"s schedule, combined with the Norilsk news, have now compounded jitters sparked by the delay in the talks.

"The possible impact from the (Norilsk) news is uncertain at this stage. In the longer term, tough competition (between multiple Russian PGM exporters) could put downward pressure on prices of the white metals. But in the shorter term, deliveries from Russia could be postponed further," one trader said.
Japanese traders said spot palladium prices have more scope to firm if the arrival of the Russian mission is postponed. "Spot palladium could reach $150 per ounce in March," Suga said.

Another bullion house official was more circumspect, saying palladium prices could rise to around $140 if no exact time was set for bilateral talks, although they could slip to $125 to $130 once a schedule was decided.

Supplies of palladium sponge, a form of the metal used in cars" catalytic converters, have become particularly tight in the global market, traders said, as the delay in Japan-Russia talks coincided with robust palladium demand from the automobile sector.
Traders said palladium sponge was trading at a premium of about $4 an ounce over the world spot palladium price.
